claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy contains dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
The internal boundaries are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile loading.
A minor interfacial-active dopant added during synthesis will segregate at lamellar colony interfaces.
Dopant segregation will chemically modify the colony interfaces and enhance their bonding.
The dopant will segregate to colony boundaries during solidification.
Dopant segregation will reduce interfacial energy.
Dopant segregation will reduce stress concentrations at colony boundaries.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion will delay microcrack initiation.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion will delay microcrack propagation.
Boundary strengthening caused by the dopant will increase tensile strength.
More uniform strain distribution caused by the interfacial modification will increase ductility.
The doped alloy will show statistically significant increases in both tensile strength and elongation to failure at room temperature relative to the undoped alloy.
The conventional coarse-lamellar baseline has high strength but limited ductility because of early microcrack initiation.
The intervention is beneficial only if the dopant segregates efficiently without forming deleterious secondary phases.
The useful dopant concentration must preserve the eutectic microstructure.
Prior findings in similar systems support beneficial interfacial modification.
The required dopant concentration and segregation efficiency remain undetermined.
The hypothesis is falsified if the doped samples fail to improve both strength and ductility significantly, or if effective segregation with enhanced cohesion is not confirmed.
